claim: Correct answers are often given as the first, fast response on trap items; slow correction is not the main source of correct final answers.
note: Independent: Bago and De Neys 2017 (a-10, c-01; b-16 is the same lab extension), Ghasemi 2022, Raoelison 2021. Ghasemi and Raoelison are snippet only. Human studies. Supports trust-first when the first answer is a learned one.

claim: On designed conflict items the intuitive answer is usually wrong (about 20-24% correct), yet reasoners show lower confidence on those items than on controls.
note: One fetched paper (De Neys 2011), two samples. Trap items are chosen to be wrong, so 20% is not a base rate.

claim: Lower confidence (feeling of rightness) in the first answer predicts more reflection and more answer changes.
note: Thompson 2011, Bago and De Neys, Pennycook 2015, all snippet. Pennycook adds that conflict detection sometimes fails. The machine analogue (agreement, token confidence) is untested.

claim: The strict fast-then-slow two-system picture is contested; revised views say heuristic and logical intuitions are both generated at once and deliberation matters mainly on conflict.
note: De Neys 2012 and 2023 versus the Melnikoff and Bargh critique, with defenders replying. Use as a design hint (check when signals conflict), not as a two-module architecture.

claim: Insight problems are solved by representational change (constraint relaxation, chunk decomposition) rather than by heuristic search.
note: Knoblich 1999, Oellinger 2006 and 2013 support it. A 2023 review (a-06, c-09) calls suddenness evidence inconclusive and subjective. Jones 2003 tested a rival. All snippet. The dispute is mostly about suddenness.

claim: Aha experience is an unreliable marker of restructuring.
note: b-22 is an unnamed search listing (credibility 35). a-06 and c-09 may share one 2023 critique. Weak.

claim: Thinking aloud or verbalizing hurts insight problems specifically.
note: Schooler 1993 found it. Gilhooly 2010 (n=80), Macchi 2025 (not opened) and Salmon-Mordekovich 2023 did not. Face verbal overshadowing replicated (Alogna 2014), so the effect is task specific.

claim: Chain-of-thought lowers accuracy on tasks where deliberation also hurts people (implicit pattern learning, some classification), by up to 36.3 points.
note: The same Liu et al. paper three times; b-04 is a secondary page with a different number. The 36.3 figure compares o1-preview with GPT-4o, so it is not a clean CoT on/off effect.

claim: Chain-of-thought helps mainly on math and symbolic tasks and gives little elsewhere; gains on planning depend on narrow prompts.
note: Sprague 2025 meta-analysis (fetched) and Stechly 2024 on Blocksworld (fetched). Supports gating deliberation by task type.

claim: Reasoning models do worse than standard models on easy problems, gain at medium, and collapse at high complexity; they overthink trivial items.
note: Shojaee 2025 (b-11 and c-15 are one paper) and Chen 2024 agree on easy-case waste. Opus and Lawsen say the high-complexity collapse is partly token limits and impossible instances. The easy-case waste is better supported than the collapse.

claim: Reasoning models often reach the right candidate in their trace but fail to endorse or keep it.
note: Mizumoto 2025 (riddles) and Cuesta-Ramirez 2025 (AIME). Both preprints. Suggests an explicit keep-or-reject step on candidates already generated.

claim: LLMs cannot reliably self-correct reasoning without external feedback; accuracy can fall.
note: Huang 2024, fetched. Other field briefs support it but it is one source in this set.

claim: LLM agents rarely build valid counterexamples to wrong solutions (under 9% for the best agent on REFUTE) even when they can solve the same problems.
note: One benchmark. Limits any counterexample-hunt step unless a code run supplies the check.

claim: Written reasoning can be unfaithful and be pushed by biasing features such as answer position (accuracy drop up to 36%).
note: Turpin 2023, fetched.

claim: External verifiers around an LLM improve planning where the LLM alone is poor (about 12% average success for GPT-4).
note: Valmeekam 2023 and 2024 are one group; Stechly 2024 is the same group. Preprints. Real independence is closer to 1.5; results agree across model generations.

claim: Search over thoughts (generate, evaluate, backtrack) beats single-pass chain of thought on search-like puzzles (Game of 24: about 4% versus 74%).
note: Yao 2023, snippet, one task, many calls.

claim: Problem solving is search through a problem space with means-ends analysis and subgoals; isomorphic problems differ in difficulty by representation.
note: Foundational book and later studies. Not an effect-size claim. Kotovsky findings not read.

claim: Scientific reasoning splits into hypothesis search and experiment search (SDDS), later extended to four spaces.
note: Klahr and Dunbar 1988 (n=20 and 10) and Schunn and Klahr 1995 are the same research line. No replication found (c-11). No LLM application found (b-21).

claim: Many thinking biases (myside, anchoring, base-rate neglect, framing) are only weakly related to intelligence, so a stronger model does not remove them.
note: Stanovich and West papers are one lab, snippet. MedEinst (preprint) suggests stronger LLMs can show higher trap rates, but the figure was not verified.

claim: Frontier LLMs keep a common first diagnosis against counterfactual evidence (an Einstellung-like trap).
note: MedEinst preprint, 5,383 cases, 17 models, fetched. Medical domain only.

claim: Models show human-like content effects in logic (better when semantics support the inference); larger models are more logical but keep human-like errors.
note: Lampinen 2024 and Eisape 2024, different labs.

claim: Early GPT models made human-like intuitive errors on cognitive reflection items; ChatGPT models mostly did not, even with chain of thought blocked.
note: Same paper twice (Hagendorff 2023). a-22 is from memory, b-15 snippet.

claim: Mental-model theory: people represent only true cases and miss false ones; mReasoner has a counterexample-search parameter.
note: Khemlani and Johnson-Laird 2017 support it. Their 2012 meta-analysis of 12 syllogism theories found none adequate. The mReasoner LLM fit is a preprint. No test that adding a counterexample step improves LLM accuracy.

claim: Self-consistency is well calibrated when the model is mostly right but amplifies confidence in systematic errors; verbalized confidence may calibrate better at lower cost.
note: Two unnamed 2026 preprint snippets, credibility 40-45, partly in conflict. Matches our own finding that correlated samples are weak evidence, but the sources are unverified.

claim: The hard-to-read font effect on Cognitive Reflection Test scores did not replicate, and the unconscious-thought advantage did not hold in a large replication or after trim-and-fill.
note: Meyer 2015 (original plus 16 replications) and Nieuwenstein 2015 (N=399 plus 61 effects). Both fetched. Do not build in disfluency or distraction-incubation tricks.
